newsitem.title: USA: AMA unveils Medicare reform plan ending "Medigap".
newsitem.headline: AMA unveils Medicare reform plan ending "Medigap".

text.p: The nation's largest doctors' group Wednesday asked Congress to act quickly to reform Medicare, unveiling its own plan that would scrap a popular type of health insurance for seniors, expand benefits and impose an up-front $500 deductible and new premiums.
Like most Medicare reform proposals of the past few years, the American Medical Association (AMA) proposed giving people a wider array of choices, including managed care plans.
But the most dramatic changes the AMA proposed envisions scrapping the "Medigap" policies that 78 percent of seniors now purchase to fill in the gaps in their Medicare coverage.
The proposal is likely to encounter opposition from the insurance industry, which has robust Medigap sales.

Instead of buying Medigap and paying an assortment of Medicare copayment fees and deductibles for health care, people would pay the roughly $1,000 they spend now for Medigap as a premium for expanded Medicare coverage.
They would also pay an up-front $500 annual deductible, the unused portion of which would be refunded.
There would be relief for low-income people. In general most people would pay about the same or less for more coverage, the AMA said.
Currently, Medicare includes a $763 deductible for hospital care. People who choose to buy optional coverage for doctors' services pay a $42.50-per-month premium.

The AMA also proposed raising Medicare eligibility to age 67 from the current 65 and increasing the amount well-off beneficiaries pay for coverage. And it opposed an idea, raised by President Clinton, of leaving major Medicare reforms to an independent commission.
"The time to do this is now. Enough putting this off ... the country is no longer in denial that we have a problem," said AMA President Daniel Johnson.

Medicare's hospital trust fund is facing bankruptcy within the next five years. Congress, which hit an impasse on politically-charged Medicare reform last year, expects to deal with it again early next year.

The AMA plan also contains a number of changes doctors have long sought, including a phase-out of price controls for Medicare services, malpractice reform and allowing doctors to set up provider networks that would compete with networks run by insurance companies.
Congressional Republicans last year proposed $270 billion in Medicare reductions as part of a balanced budget plan.

The plan was vetoed by Clinton and Democrats attacked Republicans relentlessly during the elections, accusing them of trying to gut Medicare. Still smarting, Republicans now say it is up to Clinton to recommend ways to save the program.
